title: Why Venice Is Sinking Into Its Own Lagoon
sources: Landsat imagery courtesy of the U.S. Geological Survey

paragraphs.text: On the morning of the twenty-second of November 2022, the sea off Venice rose to one hundred and seventy-three centimeters. That is the kind of tide that, three years earlier, had put most of the city under water. This time, almost nobody in Venice got their feet wet. Somewhere under the sea, something had stood up. We will get to what it was, what it cost, and why it may not be enough.

stat.label: Sea level off Venice, 22 November 2022
stat.source: Autorità per la Laguna di Venezia, MOSE log

shots.photo: File:St Mark's Square, Venice flooded by extreme midnight tide.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: St Mark's Square at high water

paragraphs.text: Venice is built on a cluster of small islands in a shallow lagoon on Italy's northeast coast. The lagoon covers about five hundred and fifty square kilometers, and it meets the Adriatic Sea through just three gaps in a long strip of sand: the Lido inlet, about eight hundred meters wide, Malamocco, about four hundred, and Chioggia, a little less. For more than a thousand years, that arrangement kept the city alive.

stat.label: The Venetian lagoon, the largest wetland in the Mediterranean

shots.photo: File:(Venice) Veduta del Canal Grande dalla Punta della Dogana - Bernardo Bellotto.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The Grand Canal, painted by Bernardo Bellotto, 18th century

paragraphs.text: But something has gone wrong. Of all the exceptional floods recorded in Venice since 1872, the ones above one hundred and forty centimeters, more than a quarter came in just two years, 2018 and 2019. The water is higher than it used to be, and the city is lower.

stat.label: Exceptional tides, recorded since 1872
stat.source: Comune di Venezia / ISPRA, tide forecasts 2021

chart.title: Exceptional tides (≥ 140 cm) in Venice
chart.source: Comune di Venezia / ISPRA, tide forecasts 2021

shots.photo: File:Canal in Venice, high water on walkway.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: High water on a canal walkway, 2024

paragraphs.text: This is the story of how that happened: rivers that were moved by hand, wells that pulled a city down, a canal dug for oil tankers, one terrible night in 1966, and a six-billion-euro machine hidden on the seabed. Why is Venice sinking into its own lagoon, and can anything stop it? The first reason lies under the city's feet.

shots.photo: File:Venice Old Town Lagoon Aerial View.jpg

chapters.title: A City on Mud and Wood

paragraphs.text: Nobody chose this place because it was easy to build on. In the fifth and sixth centuries, as the Roman world fell apart and invaders crossed northern Italy, people from the mainland towns fled into the lagoon. The marshy islands were hard to reach and hard to attack. That was the point.

stat.label: Mainland refugees settle the lagoon islands
stat.source: History of the Republic of Venice

shots.on_screen_text: Marsh islands of the Venetian lagoon

paragraphs.text: The ground was another problem. Under Venice lie layers of soft silt, sand and clay, laid down by rivers and tides. To build on it, the Venetians drove wooden piles into the mud, mostly oak and larch, packed close together, and set stone foundations on top. Many piles reach a firmer layer the Venetians called caranto: a stiff clay that dried out and hardened during the last ice age, between about eighteen and seven thousand years ago.

shots.photo: File:Venice view, Grand Canal, Venice, Italy.jpg

stat.label: The ground under the city
Driven into the mud, with stone foundations on top
Most of the piles, plus alder, pine and elm

shots.photo: File:Grand Canal Santa Maria della Salute Vaporetto Gondola Venice 01.jpg

stat.label: A stiff clay layer, dried out 18,000-7,000 years ago

shots.on_screen_text: The lagoon from the space station

paragraphs.text: The wood survives because it stays wet. Down in the waterlogged mud there is almost no oxygen, and the microbes that rot timber cannot live without it. Centuries later, much of the city still stands on those piles.

shots.photo: File:Ca' Rezzonico - Il Canal Grande verso Ca' Pesaro (Inv.219) - Ippolito Caffi.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The Grand Canal, Ippolito Caffi, 19th century

stat.label: Wet mud keeps the wood from rotting

shots.photo: File:Aerial photographs of Venice 2013, Anton Nossik, 018.jpg

paragraphs.text: But soft ground keeps settling under weight, and a lagoon is never still. The sea comes in twice a day through the three inlets. Rivers from the Alps pour fresh water and mud in from the other side. Too much mud, and the lagoon fills up and turns to land. Too much sea, and it becomes a bay. Venice needed the lagoon to stay exactly as it was. So the Venetians did something very few cities have ever tried. They moved the rivers.

shots.on_screen_text: Venice and Murano from the space station
Marsh at the lagoon's northern edge
The sea side of the lagoon

shots.photo: File:Admiralty Chart No 1483 Chioggia Malamocco Lido and Venice, Published 1893.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Venice, Lido and Malamocco, Admiralty chart of 1893

paragraphs.text: By the fifteenth century, the danger was clear. The Brenta, the Piave, the Sile and smaller rivers were dumping so much silt into the lagoon that channels were clogging and the lagoon was slowly filling in. For the Republic of Venice, a lagoon full of mud meant ships that could not reach the docks and a city no longer guarded by water.

shots.photo: File:Carte hydrographique de la Vénétie - Io. Bat. Maza f. - btv1b53170332x (2 of 3).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Hydrographic map of the Veneto, 17th century
Venice, painted by Karl Kaufmann, around 1900
Shallow flats of the southern lagoon

paragraphs.text: In 1501 the Republic created a board of three officials, the Savi alle Acque, the wise men of the waters, to run the lagoon and its rivers. A few years later a larger water council was formed, led by the Doge himself. On questions about the lagoon, the water magistrates usually had the last word, even over the mainland towns that paid the price.

stat.label: The Savi alle Acque take charge of the lagoon and its rivers

shots.photo: File:Kaart van de omgeving van Venetië, ca. 1702 Les Environs de Venise (titel op object) Les Forces de l'Europe, Asie, Afrique et Amerique, ou description des principales villes avec leurs fortification, RP-P-OB-83.034-196.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The surroundings of Venice, map of about 1702

stat.label: A larger water council, led by the Doge

shots.on_screen_text: The mainland west of the lagoon

paragraphs.text: Then came the digging. Between 1489 and 1507, the Brenta was pushed south through a new channel. Between 1554 and 1577, the Brenta and the Bacchiglione were sent out of the lagoon altogether, to the sea near Brondolo. In 1610 work began on the Taglio Novissimo, a canal that carried the Brenta and a string of smaller rivers along the lagoon's edge. In 1579 a cut called the Taglio del Re turned the Piave east toward Caorle, and in 1664 it was diverted again. In the 1680s the Sile was led into the Piave's old bed and out to sea.

shots.on_screen_text: Fusina, where the Brenta reached the lagoon

stat.label: Brenta and Bacchiglione sent to the sea near Brondolo
stat.source: Italian Ministry of Environment, lagoon chronology

stat.label: The Piave is turned east toward Caorle, twice
stat.source: Italian Ministry of Environment, lagoon chronology

arrows.label: Sile, into the old Piave bed

shots.photo: File:Map of the lagoon of Venice - Roux Joseph - 1804.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The lagoon of Venice, map of 1804

paragraphs.text: It worked. The lagoon stopped filling up, and Venice stayed an island city. But the mainland paid. Diverted rivers flooded fields and villages, and new marshes spread where the water could no longer drain. And the lagoon lost something it would need later: the mud that rivers had always brought in. A lagoon without new mud can only hold its shape if nothing else takes mud out. In the twentieth century, a lot of things did.

shots.on_screen_text: The lagoon and its inlets from Landsat
Farmland on the lagoon's mainland edge
Open flats of the central lagoon

paragraphs.text: Look across the lagoon from Venice toward the mainland and you see cranes, tanks and chimneys. That is Porto Marghera, an industrial port built on the lagoon's edge in the twentieth century. Between 1927 and 1960, about twenty-two square kilometers of salt marsh were filled in for the factories, and the airport and new districts of Mestre took several more.

stat.label: Salt marsh filled in for the industrial zone, 1927-1960
stat.source: Sarretta et al., Continental Shelf Research 2010

shots.on_screen_text: Venice airport and Mestre's lagoon edge

paragraphs.text: Industry needs water, and the cheapest water was underground. From around the 1930s, companies drilled wells into the layers of sand beneath the lagoon and pumped out fresh groundwater. The pumping peaked between 1950 and 1970.

stat.label: Industrial wells tap the groundwater under the lagoon
Peak years of groundwater pumping

paragraphs.text: Here is the trouble with taking water out of the ground. In soft layers of sand and clay, the water helps hold the grains apart. Pump it out, and the layers squeeze together, and everything on top goes down with them. Between 1950 and 1970, Venice sank by about twelve centimeters, in twenty years. At the peak, the city was dropping about five millimeters a year, several times faster than the slow natural settling.

stat.label: Groundwater keeps the grains of sand and clay apart
Take the water out, and the ground compacts
Sinking of Venice at the peak of pumping

paragraphs.text: It took years to stop it. In the early 1970s the wells were closed by law, and the sinking slowed sharply, to about a tenth of the rate of those twenty years. But the twelve centimeters never came back. Compacted clay does not spring up again. Venice was permanently lower, just as the sea was starting to rise. And Marghera had brought something else to the lagoon: ships far bigger than anything the old channels could carry.

stat.label: The wells are closed by law; sinking drops to about a tenth

shots.photo: File:Signe Acqua Alta 1966 - Cloître monastère San Lazzaro décembre 2022.JPG
File:ISS046-E-45729 - View of Italy - Venetian lagoon - San Giorgio in Meergras-Alga - Canale di Malamocco-Marghera - Fusina - Moranzani - Casse di colmata - Canale Avesa (cropped).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The Malamocco-Marghera canal from the space station

paragraphs.text: The refineries needed tankers, and tankers needed deep water. In the 1960s, engineers dug the Malamocco-Marghera ship canal, known in Venice as the Oil Canal. It runs from the Malamocco inlet straight across the middle of the lagoon to the industrial port. You can see it from space: a dark, straight line through water that is mostly knee-deep.

shots.on_screen_text: The canal at the Malamocco inlet
The Oil Canal across the central lagoon
The lagoon from the space station, 2016

paragraphs.text: Digging it moved more than forty million cubic meters of sediment, and much of that was dumped on land, out of the lagoon for good. Worse, the straight, deep channel changed how water moves. Tides and waves pushed into the central lagoon with more force, stirring up the mud on the shallow flats and carrying it out to sea.

stat.label: Sediment dug out for the Oil Canal, much of it dumped on land
stat.source: Sarretta et al., Continental Shelf Research 2010

shots.on_screen_text: The canal and the shallows around it
Muddy water on the central flats

paragraphs.text: Scientists who compared depth surveys of the whole lagoon from 1927, 1970 and 2002 found what that meant. The lagoon lost about one hundred and ten million cubic meters of sediment over those seventy-five years. Its typical depth went from sixty-two centimeters to eighty-eight. The area of open flats between seventy-five centimeters and two meters deep more than doubled, from eighty-eight square kilometers to two hundred and six. Salt marshes, the low green islands that break the waves, shrank from sixty-eight square kilometers to thirty-two, less than half. In the later decades, clam fishing on the lagoon bed stirred up even more mud, and the yearly loss rose from point three to point eight million cubic meters.

stat.label: Sediment lost by the lagoon, 1927-2002
stat.source: Sarretta et al., Continental Shelf Research 2010

paragraphs.text: In those surveys, the lagoon was turning into something else: deeper, more open, more like a bay of the sea. The researchers described it as starved of sediment. A deeper lagoon lets tides in faster and lets storms build bigger waves. And a city that had already sunk now sat in a lagoon that was losing its defenses. All it needed was the right storm.

stat.label: How the 2010 study described the lagoon
stat.source: Sarretta et al., Continental Shelf Research 2010

paragraphs.text: On the third and fourth of November 1966, a deep low-pressure system sat over the Mediterranean, and the scirocco, the warm southeast wind, blew straight up the Adriatic for hours. It piled the sea against the top of the Adriatic, right where Venice sits. On the morning of the fourth, the sea broke through the stone sea walls at Pellestrina, the thin strip of land that shields the lagoon, in three places.

stat.label: Low pressure and a scirocco storm

paragraphs.text: The tide in Venice reached one hundred and ninety-four centimeters above the city's old reference mark, the highest ever recorded there. On the city's own flood table, that level puts about nine tenths of its streets and squares under water. Electricity failed across the whole city, hospitals included. Heating oil leaked from flooded tanks and spread through the streets and canals. More than two thousand shops and workshops were damaged, and many never reopened. That evening, the hospital on the Lido counted eight hundred people who had fled the flooded island of Pellestrina.

stat.label: Venice, 4 November 1966: the highest tide on record

shots.photo: File:Piazzetta San Marco - alluvione di Venezia 1966.jpg

stat.label: Of the city's walkways under water at that level
Shops and workshops damaged

paragraphs.text: The world noticed. In 1973 Italy passed a special law declaring the protection of Venice and its lagoon a matter of primary national interest. That law started half a century of plans, arguments and money that led, eventually, to MOSE. But the water did not wait.

shots.photo: File:L'inondation de 1966 à Venise (exposition sur le projet Mose, Venise) (35696067702).jpg

stat.label: Italy's Special Law for Venice

document.text: Law 171 of 16 April 1973: the safeguarding of Venice and its lagoon is of primary national interest.
document.title: Special Law for Venice

paragraphs.text: Venice measures every tide against a mark set at Punta della Salute in 1897. Since then the average sea level has risen to about thirty-two centimeters above that mark. A study of a century and a half of records found that roughly half of that rise came from the sea itself, and the other half from Venice sinking. Every centimeter lost on either side means the same storm floods more of the city.

stat.label: Average sea level above the 1897 mark (2021)
stat.source: Comune di Venezia / ISPRA, tide forecasts 2021

chart.title: Why the water is higher at Venice, 1872-2019

shots.on_screen_text: St Mark's Square at high water

paragraphs.text: The city keeps a table of what each tide does. At ninety centimeters, about two percent of the streets and squares are wet, mostly around Saint Mark's Square, the lowest part of town. At one hundred and ten, twelve percent. At one hundred and twenty, more than a quarter. At one hundred and forty, fifty-nine percent. Each step of ten centimeters floods a new ring of streets, so a city that loses ten centimeters to the sea gets every flood one step worse. In August 2020 the tide reached one hundred and three centimeters, the highest August tide since records began in 1872.

stat.label: Walkways under water at a 90 cm tide

shots.on_screen_text: The lowest streets, around St Mark's

chart.title: Share of Venice's walkways under water

stat.label: 30 August 2020, the highest August tide since 1872

paragraphs.text: Then came 2019. On the twelfth of November, four things came together. It was a spring tide, when the sun and the moon pull together. The whole northern Adriatic was running high: that November the average sea level in Venice was almost thirty centimeters above normal. The scirocco was blowing up the Adriatic. And that evening a small, intense low formed over the northern Adriatic and drove a local wind of about a hundred kilometers an hour across the lagoon, with gusts of a hundred and ten. City workers at San Zaccaria, on the waterfront, said they heard a roar just before the gust hit them. The tide reached one hundred and eighty-seven centimeters, the second highest ever recorded, and almost ninety percent of the city went under water. That year Venice had twenty-eight tides of one hundred and ten centimeters or more, the level where the sirens sound. Five tides reached one hundred and forty, and the records had never shown more than two in a single year. Three of them came within six days. In that November alone, the water stood above one hundred and ten centimeters for about fifty hours. The previous record for a November was about twenty-four. Tides once rare enough to be remembered by their dates were becoming a season.

paragraphs.text: The answer Italy built is called MOSE, a name taken from Moses, who parted the sea. Construction began in 2003. At each of the three inlets, rows of steel gates lie flat on the seabed, hollow boxes filled with water. There are seventy-eight of them in four barriers: twenty-one and twenty at the Lido inlet, joined by an artificial island built in the middle of the channel, nineteen at Malamocco and eighteen at Chioggia. Each gate is twenty meters wide and up to about twenty-nine meters long.

shots.on_screen_text: The MOSE exhibition at the Arsenale

stat.label: MOSE construction begins

shots.on_screen_text: A MOSE gate in its seabed housing, exhibition panel
A gate at work: sign at the Lido inlet, 2017
The artificial island between the Lido barriers

stat.label: Width × length of the biggest gates

paragraphs.text: When a tide above one hundred and ten centimeters is forecast, compressed air pushes the water out of the gates. They swing up on their hinges until they stand above the waves, and the lagoon is shut off from the sea. When the tide falls, water is let back in and the gates sink out of sight.

stat.label: Forecast tide that raises the gates
stat.source: Autorità per la Laguna di Venezia, MOSE log

paragraphs.text: Getting there was a scandal. In June 2014, police arrested thirty-five people over contracts for the project, among them the mayor of Venice, Giorgio Orsoni, who resigned days later. The bill came to about six billion euros in today's money. All seventy-eight gates were raised together for the first time in a test in July 2020. On the third of October 2020, they went up for a real tide.

stat.label: June 2014, including the mayor of Venice

paragraphs.text: Since then, they have gone up again and again: twenty times in the first season, thirteen, nineteen, thirty-two, twenty-three, and then forty-nine times in the season that ended in May 2026, thirty of them in January and February alone. By November 2026 the count had passed one hundred and sixty. On the twenty-second of November 2022, the morning with the one hundred and seventy-three centimeter tide from the start of this video, all four barriers were up, and the city stayed mostly dry. Outside the gates, the gauges at the inlets read one hundred and eighty-seven centimeters at the Lido, one hundred and ninety-one at Chioggia, and two hundred and four at Malamocco. On the city's own table, a tide like that would have flooded around four fifths of Venice.

paragraphs.text: But every closure cuts the lagoon off from the sea that keeps it alive. The tide is what flushes the lagoon, and ships need the inlets open. As the sea rises, the gates will have to close more often and for longer, perhaps for weeks each year. A barrier built for rare emergencies is turning into a wall that is up more and more often.

paragraphs.text: How long can this last? A review of Venice's sea-level records puts the likely rise from climate change by 2100 somewhere between eleven centimeters and more than a meter. In April 2026, three climate-adaptation researchers looked at every plan to save the city. They found four paths. Keep MOSE and add new tricks to it. Build ring dikes around the city itself, for up to four and a half billion euros. Seal off the whole lagoon behind a giant levee and pump it day and night, for more than thirty billion, at the cost of the living lagoon. Or, if the sea rises by several meters over the coming centuries, move people inland, for up to a hundred billion.

paragraphs.text: One of the new tricks would turn the old mistake around. Instead of pumping water out from under Venice, pump seawater back in, deep underground. A 2011 study by Pietro Teatini and his colleagues modeled twelve wells in a ring around the city and found the ground could rise by about twenty-five to thirty centimeters over ten years. Other scientists have warned that it needs far more testing first. If it works, the review found, the gates might hold even after a meter of sea-level rise. After that, the choices get much harder.

stat.label: Modelled uplift in 10 years from 12 seawater wells (2011)
Critics ask for far more study before injecting

paragraphs.text: Meanwhile, the people are leaving. In 1951, one hundred and seventy-four thousand eight hundred and eight people lived in historic Venice. Ten years later it was a hundred and forty-five thousand, by 1971 a hundred and eight thousand, and by 2015 fifty-five thousand. At the end of 2024 the city counted forty-eight thousand four hundred and eighty-nine. Venice may stay above the water. Whether it stays a city is another question.

paragraphs.text: If you were in charge of Venice, would you keep closing the gates, or seal the lagoon for good and lose what made it Venice?

ask.text: Keep closing the gates, or seal the lagoon for good?

youtube.title: Why Venice Is Sinking Into Its Own Lagoon
youtube.description: Venice is lower than it used to be and the sea is higher. This video follows how that happened: the wooden piles under the city, the rivers the Venetian Republic moved by hand, the industrial wells that sank the city twelve centimeters in twenty years, the oil-tanker canal that helped empty the lagoon of mud, the floods of 1966 and 2019, and MOSE, the 78 steel gates that now rise from the seabed. And what comes after them.
